name: Platform-Neutral Authentication Framework
consequences: Establishing open-standard authentication reduces reliance on proprietary OS signals but requires redefining trust metrics without platform-specific telemetry. This shifts friction from technical integration to regulatory acceptance of alternative verification criteria.
options: Deploy FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS with hardware-backed attestation
Design browser-based token authentication using OpenID Connect and WebAuthn
Integrate hardware security modules (HSMs) for decentralized credential validation
review: Adopting FIDO2 risks slow adoption without platform vendor alignment, while HSMs introduce infrastructure complexity that may deter public-sector procurement.

name: Procurement-Driven Standards Pressure
consequences: Mandating platform-neutral requirements in AltID contracts forces technical compliance but faces resistance from incumbents prioritizing ecosystem integration. This creates a feedback loop where regulatory language shapes architectural choices.
options: Draft procurement clauses requiring fallback authentication paths in all digital-service contracts
Leverage EU eIDAS2 compliance frameworks to standardize interoperability requirements
Partner with public-sector buyers to co-develop procurement templates prioritizing open standards
review: Procurement mandates risk being circumvented through loophole-driven contract language, requiring continuous alignment with evolving regulatory interpretations.

name: Coalition-Driven Policy Framing
consequences: Building cross-sector alliances amplifies advocacy reach but dilutes focus on technical specificity. Success depends on maintaining credibility with both technologists and policymakers through shared metrics.
options: Form a consortium with civil-society privacy groups and academic researchers to co-author policy briefs
Engage Folketinget's digital policy committee through targeted legislative impact assessments
Create a joint industry-academia task force to publish independent risk analyses of platform dependency
review: Coalition-building risks prioritizing consensus over technical rigor, particularly when aligning privacy advocacy with procurement realities.

name: Technical Demonstrator Ecosystem
consequences: Non-production demonstrators validate feasibility but require careful scope definition to avoid being dismissed as academic exercises. Their impact depends on tangible links to procurement timelines.
options: Build a FIDO2-compatible demo for public healthcare portal access with minimal UI changes
Develop a browser-based authentication prototype using WebAuthn and decentralized identifiers (DIDs)
Create a hardware-token proof-of-concept compatible with existing MitID infrastructure
review: Demonstrators may lack immediate utility for public-sector adopters unless they align with existing migration pathways for legacy systems.

name: EU Standards Alignment Strategy
consequences: Tying Danish proposals to European Digital Identity Wallet frameworks increases credibility but requires navigating conflicting regional priorities. This creates leverage through broader interoperability demands.
options: Contribute to ETSI/ENISA working groups on platform-neutral authentication standards
Map AltID requirements to upcoming eIDAS3 interoperability mandates
Lobby for inclusion of fallback-path criteria in the European Digital Identity Framework
review: EU alignment risks dilution of national priorities if European bodies prioritize vendor-neutral frameworks over specific Danish contingency needs.

name: Regulatory Fallback Mandates
consequences: Imposing legal requirements for fallback authentication paths could force platform neutrality but risks litigation from Apple/Google. Downstream, it may accelerate alternative standard adoption but could also trigger retaliatory policy shifts by foreign regulators.
options: Draft procurement clauses requiring fallback authentication in public-sector contracts
Leverage eIDAS2 framework to mandate platform-neutral identity verification
Establish a public-private certification body for alternative authentication methods
review: Mandating fallbacks could face legal challenges from platform providers, delaying implementation while creating compliance uncertainty for public-sector adopters.

name: Cross-Platform Certification Authority
consequences: Creating a multi-stakeholder certification body could standardize alternatives but requires consensus among competitors. Downstream, it might reduce technical fragmentation but could also entrench new monopolies if governance is captured.
options: Develop a neutral certification framework for non-platform-specific authentication
Partner with Nordic regulatory bodies to validate alternative trust models
Create a sandbox environment for testing platform-neutral authentication protocols
review: Establishing a new certification body may struggle with credibility and resource allocation, risking duplication of existing standards efforts.

name: Geopolitical Risk Mitigation Framework
consequences: Prioritizing geographically diversified authentication infrastructure could reduce dependency risks but requires significant investment. Downstream, it may improve resilience but could also fragment technical standards across regions.
options: Invest in local data-center partnerships for alternative authentication backends
Diversify supplier relationships across non-English-speaking tech ecosystems
Develop contingency plans for platform-specific service disruptions
review: Geopolitical diversification may complicate technical integration and increase operational complexity without clear immediate benefits.

name: Public-Private Resilience Partnerships
consequences: Forming alliances between government and private sector could pool resources for alternative solutions but risks conflicting priorities. Downstream, it may accelerate development but could also create dependency on corporate partners.
options: Create joint task forces with financial institutions to test alternative authentication models
Establish shared risk-assessment frameworks for digital identity continuity
Co-fund research initiatives with tech startups specializing in platform-neutral solutions
review: Aligning private sector incentives with public goals may dilute the project's sovereignty objectives and create new points of vulnerability.

name: Citizen-Driven Authentication Trials
consequences: Engaging citizens in testing alternatives could build grassroots support but may reveal usability challenges. Downstream, it might pressure policymakers but could also expose vulnerabilities in unproven systems.
options: Launch beta programs with specific demographic groups for alternative authentication methods
Implement feedback loops with privacy advocates to refine fallback solutions
Conduct community workshops to co-design platform-neutral identity workflows
review: Citizen trials may highlight practical limitations of alternatives, requiring significant rework before institutional adoption.

name: EU Interoperability Advocacy
consequences: Pushing for European-wide standards could amplify Denmark's influence but requires navigating complex EU politics. Downstream, it may create scalable solutions but could also delay local implementation.
options: Influence European Digital Identity Wallet specifications to include fallback requirements
Collaborate with EU member states on cross-border authentication resilience
Lobby for harmonized procurement rules across Nordic countries
review: EU advocacy risks diluting Denmark's specific needs in favor of broader compromises, potentially weakening targeted reforms.

name: Open-Source Identity Integration
consequences: Building on open-source platforms could reduce vendor lock-in but requires sustained community engagement. Downstream, it may foster innovation but could also lead to fragmented implementations.
options: Develop open-source authentication modules compatible with multiple OS ecosystems
Collaborate with Linux distributions to integrate platform-neutral identity solutions
Create a public repository for alternative authentication protocols and test cases
review: Open-source approaches may lack the commercial support needed for critical infrastructure, increasing maintenance risks over time.

name: Stakeholder Coalition Expansion
consequences: Broadening coalition membership increases influence but risks diluting focus. A diverse coalition may accelerate policy traction but requires managing conflicting priorities among civil society, industry, and government stakeholders. Sustained engagement is critical to maintain momentum through institutional inertia.
options: Forming cross-sector alliances with private and public entities
Engaging civil society for grassroots advocacy
Establishing academic partnerships for technical validation
review: Overextending coalition scope risks fragmentation; success depends on maintaining a cohesive core while leveraging peripheral allies.

name: Alternative Authentication Protocols
consequences: Adopting non-platform-specific protocols enhances resilience but faces resistance from existing system integrators. Technical validation is required to prove viability, while regulatory alignment ensures adoption. Early standardization efforts could lock in competing architectures.
options: Implementing FIDO2-based solutions for decentralized authentication
Exploring blockchain for tamper-resistant identity verification
Developing hardware token standards for offline access
review: Novel protocols require both technical credibility and regulatory buy-in, creating a high-barrier entry for disruptive alternatives.

name: Regulatory Advocacy Channels
consequences: Direct policy engagement accelerates institutional change but demands sustained resource allocation. Early alignment with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen could shape procurement requirements, while EU-level advocacy risks dilution through broader stakeholder interests.
options: Lobbying for policy changes in Digitaliseringsstyrelsen
Engaging with EU regulatory bodies on interoperability standards
Publishing white papers to influence public discourse
review: Regulatory influence is slow and contested; success hinges on combining technical evidence with political timing.

name: Public Sector Pilot Programs
consequences: Testing fallback mechanisms in real-world scenarios validates technical approaches but limits scope to non-critical services. Pilot success could justify broader adoption, while failure risks credibility loss and increased scrutiny.
options: Piloting fallback mechanisms in non-critical public services
Collaborating with local municipalities for decentralized testing
Testing with public healthcare systems for high-security validation
review: Pilots risk being perceived as low-impact if not strategically scaled, requiring careful selection of use cases.

name: International Compliance Alignment
consequences: Aligning with global standards enhances credibility but introduces complexity in local adaptation. EU-level advocacy could create synergies, while diverging from international norms risks isolation and reduced interoperability.
options: Adopting ISO standards for identity management frameworks
Participating in global cybersecurity policy forums
Aligning with GDPR for data sovereignty requirements
review: Global alignment demands balancing international best practices with local regulatory specificity, risking misalignment in critical areas.

name: Security Certification Pathways
consequences: Establishing new certification processes strengthens trust but delays deployment. Certification bodies may resist changes that undermine existing platform-centric models, creating bottlenecks for alternative solutions.
options: Creating a national certification body for platform-neutral systems
Partnering with existing certification agencies for hybrid validation
Developing self-assessment frameworks for rapid iteration
review: Certification hurdles could stall progress; success depends on convincing regulators to prioritize resilience over convenience.

name: Vendor Diversification Strategies
consequences: Encouraging local and open-source vendors reduces dependency but requires nurturing nascent ecosystems. Multi-vendor procurement policies face resistance from entrenched suppliers, while open-source solutions demand sustained community investment.
options: Encouraging local tech vendors through public procurement incentives
Promoting open-source identity solutions for transparency
Establishing multi-vendor procurement policies for critical systems
review: Diversification risks underdeveloped alternatives; success depends on balancing immediate needs with long-term ecosystem growth.
